title: An understanding heart (1 Kings 3:5–9)
hook: offered anything, Solomon asks for "an understanding heart", literally a listening heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's last words: one who rules justly is like the light of morning. Today a new book, Kings, opens, and a new king is asked a strange question.

"Ask what I shall give thee." That's the whole offer. Solomon, David's son, is newly king, and he has gone to Gibeon to bring offerings. That night, the text says, the LORD appears to him in a dream and speaks those words. No limits, no conditions. In the old wish stories, this is where people ask for gold, or long life, or for their enemies to vanish. Solomon's answer is short and odd. He calls himself a little child who doesn't know how to go out or come in. He has a great people to lead, and he knows he isn't ready. So he asks for one thing.
screen: `A DREAM AT GIBEON.` → `ASK WHAT I SHALL GIVE THEE.` → `I AM BUT A LITTLE CHILD.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, Solomon asks for "an understanding heart to judge Thy people." The Hebrew is plainer, and stranger: lev shomea. Lev is heart. Shomea is hearing, the same verb as shema in Deuteronomy's Hear, O Israel. A hearing heart. A listening heart. Notice what he leaves out, because the text lists it: God is pleased that he didn't ask for long life, or riches, or the life of his enemies, but for understanding to discern what is just. And the answer comes back larger than the request: the wisdom, and also the riches and honor he never asked for. Why listening? Solomon's job is to judge, to sit with people's disputes and decide them. A judge can be clever, quick and eloquent, and still never really hear the person in front of him. Some readers point out that in the Hebrew Bible the heart isn't only where feelings live; it's also where a person thinks and decides. So a listening heart is a mind that takes in before it rules. There's humility in it, too. He doesn't ask to be wise. He asks to be able to hear. In this story, wisdom starts with the ears.
screen: `AN UNDERSTANDING HEART.` · `LEV SHOMEA: A HEARING HEART.` · `NOT RICHES, NOT LONG LIFE.` · `WISDOM STARTS WITH THE EARS.` · then, large: `AN UNDERSTANDING HEART TO JUDGE THY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Think of one decision or conversation waiting for you, at work or at home, and before you plan what you'll say, ask what you haven't heard yet: whose side haven't you listened to all the way through? If you pray, you can borrow Solomon's words and ask for an understanding heart; if you don't, just let your listening widen for a minute.
Lev shomea. The Hebrew for a hearing heart, the only thing Solomon asked for when he could have had anything. Today's word.
Your line: a listening heart. Of everything on offer, Solomon chose to hear. Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Jews read Solomon's dream at Gibeon in the book of Kings, among the Former Prophets; some teachers use the Hebrew phrase lev shomea, a listening heart, as a picture of good judgment.
